meta.title: Listening to Ohio
meta.summary: Shh, there’s a frog in this part. A canal song, a Columbus conversation, a marsh: come get to know Ohio by ear with me.

recommendations.reason: Turn it up a little. Cleveland’s rock legacy is one way into Ohio’s music story, but local stages, recordings, and the people in the crowd keep it moving.
Drive across Ohio and listen closely: the vowels have their own geography. A state border doesn’t give everyone the same accent. Wouldn’t a little variety make the conversation more interesting?
One grand building, so many kinds of sound. I’ll take you beyond the facade to see how Cincinnati keeps Music Hall alive.

blocks.text: Listen with me for a minute? There’s a canal song I’d like to start with, a conversation in Columbus, and—ooh, wait until we get to the frogs at Beaver Marsh. I like how a place changes when we stop looking for a moment and pay attention to what we can hear. Let’s give each sound a little room.

I’d begin in Akron in the 1930s, with Captain Pearl R. Nye. He was born and raised on a canal boat; John A. Lomax and Alan and Elizabeth Lomax recorded his singing. The Library of Congress collection holds 22 audio discs with 75 songs, plus manuscripts, letters, and photographs. One person’s voice, with so much kept around it. Let’s hear him as a person telling part of the Ohio and Erie Canal’s story.

blocks.title: A song carried along the canal

blocks.text: Pick one linked recording and keep its catalog entry beside it. Who’s singing, what’s the song, which disc and side? Then listen again. I find myself wondering who taught Nye the song and how it changed along the way. The recording gives us one performance; the song texts and photographs offer more clues without settling every question.

I’d keep the people making the recording in mind too. The Lomaxes’ equipment, travels, and collecting choices shaped what reached the disc. The Library identifies these as Nye’s performances recorded in Akron. We can enjoy hearing him and still wonder about other singers whose voices weren’t captured here.

blocks.transcript: No spoken narration. The soundtrack includes insects, frogs, birds, and occasional muffled visitor voices at Beaver Marsh.

blocks.text: Now, a quieter invitation. The National Park Service’s Beaver Marsh scene has no spoken narration. Its description mentions insects, frogs, birds, and occasional muffled visitor voices. Oh, I like being left a little room to listen for myself. Animals and people share this soundscape, even when the people are somewhere in the background.

The Beaver Marsh recording includes muffled visitors’ voices among the insects, frogs, and birds. I like listening to the background after the louder sounds feel familiar. Oh, did you catch that part too?
blocks.title: Listen behind the frogs
A city has more than one voice

blocks.text: What about ordinary conversation? Ohio State researchers’ Buckeye Speech Corpus holds recordings with 40 Columbus speakers and an interviewer. The words are transcribed, phonetically labeled, and aligned with the audio. I’d follow a short stretch with the transcript open. It helps us hear a pronunciation inside the conversation where it happened.

Forty people in Columbus can’t give us every Ohio voice. That’s part of why I like comparing the speakers instead of hunting for one official-sounding accent. Who’s talking, to whom, and about what? Listen for the differences. Nobody needs to put on somebody else’s voice to be curious about it.

And now a room full of sound. Cincinnati Music Hall opened in 1878 for music and industrial exhibitions. Cincinnati Arts lists the Symphony Orchestra, Pops, Ballet, Opera, and May Festival among the organizations based there. I’d be looking forward to the performance, of course. But the rehearsals, instruments, stage work, schedules, and musicians’ livelihoods belong to the evening too.

That work has a long local history. AFM Local 1 says Cincinnati’s Musicians’ Protective Union was incorporated in 1881 and became an American Federation of Musicians local in 1897. Its constitution describes personal contracts and a master agreement for Cincinnati Symphony musicians, including rates, conditions, and touring. These are the union’s own rules. Read them beside Music Hall’s history and you can see more of the working day behind the sound we hear from a seat.

Here’s the listening order I’d choose: a Pearl Nye recording with its related records, two voices from the Buckeye Corpus, then a current Cincinnati performance listing. Stay with whatever catches your ear. For the concert, notice the ensemble and people credited too. An archived performance, a conversation, a scheduled evening—each brings us close in a different way.

A remembered song, a turn of phrase, an insect among the frogs, musicians finding a shared sound… ah, I don’t think I could choose just one way for Ohio to sound. Give each its own moment. I’d like to hear which detail you carry away.
Which sound would you stay with a little longer? Pick yours. I’ll be quiet beside you for this part. ♡
